analysis.one_liner: Funds a large expansion of homelessness programs through new taxes on mass landlords, luxury property sales, and anonymous shell-company deals.
analysis.headline: Introduced in March 2020 with 15 Democratic cosponsors, the bill sat in five House committees and never received a hearing or a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would dramatically expand federal programs for homeless and housing-unstable people: roughly $10 billion a year each for emergency shelter and permanent-housing grants, a new $6 billion block grant that can build affordable housing and public bathrooms, money for libraries that serve homeless people, and grants to help homeless people vote. It pays for this with new taxes: 5% on sales of property worth $10 million or more, 10% on real estate deals involving anonymous shell companies, 1% on rents charged by landlords who own over 1,000 units in a metro area, and a ten-year phase-out of the mortgage interest deduction. Cities that want the money would have to stop criminalizing sleeping outside and protect homeless people's belongings from being thrown away.
analysis.who_benefits: People who are homeless or close to it: more shelter beds, more permanent supportive housing, new affordable housing construction, public bathrooms and water fountains, library programs, help replacing lost ID documents, and voting access grants. Cities get funding for mental-health crisis teams and pre-arrest diversion programs instead of arrests. Renters in high-cost areas benefit from new affordable supply and from pressure on large landlords (the 1% rent tax disappears in places with rent control or just-cause eviction laws).

how_it_helps.text: Creates a new Community Development Block Grant Plus program (authorized at $6 billion a year) that cities may use to build permanently affordable housing, tiny homes, public bathrooms, and other basic infrastructure for homeless and cost-burdened households.

Authorizes up to $10 billion a year each for the Emergency Solutions Grant and Continuum of Care homeless programs (tax revenue counts toward that amount, with general funds topping up the difference), plus $1 billion a year for FEMA emergency food and shelter grants.

Bars federal homelessness money from any city that enforces laws punishing homeless people for sleeping outside and that lacks due-process protections for homeless people's property, and waives local matching-fund requirements for cities that adopt a Housing First approach.

Creates grants and studies to remove barriers to voting for homeless people, including the effect of voter ID and REAL ID rules on people without fixed addresses, plus grants for libraries to serve homeless patrons and a GAO study of barriers to replacing essential documents like ID cards.
Authorizes $100 million a year for alternatives to jailing homeless people, including mobile mental-health crisis teams and pre-arrest diversion programs.

analysis.who_pays: Sellers and buyers of high-end real estate (a 5% tax on sales of $10 million or more), parties using anonymous shell companies to hide real estate ownership (a 10% transfer tax), corporate landlords with portfolios over 1,000 units in one metro or 2,000 units overall (a 1% tax on rent collected), and homeowners claiming the mortgage interest deduction, which would shrink each year until it disappears in 2030 — a deduction that mostly goes to higher-income households with large mortgages.
analysis.who_pays_short: Luxury real estate, big landlords, wealthy homeowners

drawbacks.text: The 1% rent tax on large landlords could be passed through to tenants as higher rents, since the tax applies to the rent actually paid; the bill only waives it where rent control or just-cause eviction laws exist.
The mortgage interest deduction phase-down would raise taxes for many middle-income homeowners who itemize, not just the wealthiest, as the deduction shrinks 10% a year to zero by 2030.

The total price is enormous — well over $20 billion a year in authorized homelessness and housing spending — and the conditions tying federal money to local enforcement choices would mark a major shift of federal power over city policing and camping policies, which opponents would call federal overreach.

The anonymous-entity tax carves out entities that simply register in the legal entity identifier program, which could let some buyers of secrecy avoid the tax by a paperwork change rather than actual disclosure.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are concrete and aimed at one of the country's most visible hardships — an estimated 570,000+ people homeless on any given night — and the bill pays for them with taxes concentrated on luxury transactions and large landlords rather than broad tax increases. The real costs are the pass-through risk to renters from the landlord tax, the phase-out of a deduction many ordinary homeowners use, and the sheer scale of the spending, which made the bill a statement of principle more than a near-term plan. It was never costed or marked up, so implementation questions (like how the IRS would identify anonymous entities) were never worked through.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to five House committees the day it was introduced, none of which took it up, and it died there when the Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

narrative.text: Rep. Pramila Jayapal introduced the bill on March 19, 2020, with seven original cosponsors, and it was referred to the Financial Services, House Administration, Education and Labor, Ways and Means, and Judiciary committees.
Fifteen House Democrats signed on as cosponsors; no Republican did.
The bill received no further action after referral — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor vote — and expired when the 116th Congress ended.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large landlords, luxury property sellers, and buyers using anonymous shell companies never faced the new taxes, and federal homelessness funding stayed at its previous levels. Homeless and housing-unstable people gained nothing from the bill's failure.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large landlords and luxury real estate sellers

sides.party_line_note: All 15 cosponsors were Democrats and none of the 197 House Republicans signed on; the bill never reached the floor, so no roll-call vote ever tested the divide.

industries.note: A 1% tax on rent collected would hit landlords owning over 1,000 units in one metro area, 2,000 units overall, or 500+ units across three states. The tax is waived where rent control, just-cause eviction, or source-of-income laws exist, so the bill pays landlords to accept tenant protections.
A 5% tax on sales of property worth $10 million or more would raise the cost of high-end deals, with proceeds funding homelessness programs.

A 10% tax on property transfers involving entities whose true owners are not in public records targets hidden real estate ownership, unless the entity registers in the legal entity identifier program.
The mortgage interest deduction, which disproportionately benefits households with large mortgages, would shrink 10% a year until it is fully phased out in 2030.

industries.industry: Homeless services and affordable housing nonprofits
industries.note: The bill routes billions through shelter providers, supportive-housing operators, libraries, and voting-access nonprofits, with training and community-participation requirements attached to the money.
